contentBoundary: Topic copy is data. The symptom checklist is client-owned reference data; rule evaluation remains executable behavior in crates/msc-domain/src/router/troubleshooting.rs and fallback_tree.rs.

symptoms.title: No one can connect from outside your network
symptoms.description: The server may work locally, but internet players still cannot join.

symptoms.title: It works on the local network but not from the internet
symptoms.description: This often means the server itself is running, but upstream networking is still wrong.

symptoms.title: The router rule points to an old local IP
symptoms.description: The forwarding rule still targets a previous address instead of the host Mac's current address.

symptoms.title: The Mac's IP changed
symptoms.description: DHCP may have given the Mac a new local address.

symptoms.title: The wrong target device was selected
symptoms.description: The forwarding rule may target another Mac, PC, console, or stale DHCP entry.

symptoms.title: You forwarded on the provider device, but your own router is also present
symptoms.description: The upstream provider box may not be the device doing LAN routing.

symptoms.title: You forwarded on your own router, but provider gateway hardware is also present
symptoms.description: The provider gateway may still be doing routing unless bridge mode is enabled.

symptoms.title: Two routers or router-like devices are present
symptoms.description: Common examples include ISP gateway + personal router or gateway + mesh system.

symptoms.title: The router WAN IP does not match the public IP
symptoms.description: This can indicate CGNAT or another upstream routing layer.

symptoms.title: You are on an apartment, dorm, campus, or managed network
symptoms.description: Those environments often block direct forwarding or do not give router admin access.

symptoms.title: You do not have router admin access
symptoms.description: Without admin access, you may not be allowed to create or edit forwarding rules.

symptoms.title: Java works but Bedrock fails
symptoms.description: The Bedrock port and protocol are often different from Java.

symptoms.title: Bedrock works but Java fails
symptoms.description: The Java side may be missing its TCP rule or using the wrong target.

symptoms.title: You saw a macOS firewall or permission prompt
symptoms.description: The host may still be blocking inbound traffic even if the router rule is correct.

symptoms.title: Another security or network tool may be blocking traffic
symptoms.description: Third-party security tools can override otherwise correct routing.

symptoms.title: You saved the rule, but it still does not work
symptoms.description: Some routers need Apply, reboot, or a short delay before the rule becomes active.

symptoms.title: The router asked to reboot or apply changes
symptoms.description: The new rule may not be active yet.

symptoms.title: Your mesh or router may be in bridge / AP mode
symptoms.description: If the device is not routing, forwarding must happen elsewhere.

suggestedNextActions: Check the Mac's current local IP in the app.
Update the router rule so it points to the current local IP.
Reserve the Mac's IP in the router later so it stops changing.
topics.summary: Your router may still be forwarding to an old device address.
topics.title: Your Mac's local IP changed

suggestedNextActions: Check whether your ISP device and your own router are both doing routing.
If possible, put one device into bridge / passthrough mode.
Otherwise forward on the upstream router as well.
topics.summary: Port forwarding on the wrong router will not expose the server to the internet.
topics.title: You may be behind two routers

suggestedNextActions: Compare the router WAN IP with your public IP.
Ask the ISP whether they offer a public IP option.
Use an alternative remote-access method if needed.
topics.summary: Some internet plans do not give you a public IPv4 address you can forward through.
topics.title: Your ISP may be using CGNAT

suggestedNextActions: Find which device is acting as the main router.
If you use mesh, open the mesh app first.
If your own router is connected to ISP hardware, configure the router that owns the LAN.
topics.summary: The provider name is not always the router actually doing the routing.
topics.title: You configured the wrong device

suggestedNextActions: Confirm the selected target device matches the host Mac.
Use the detected local IP from the app when possible.
Delete duplicate rules that point to old devices.
topics.summary: The rule must target the Mac that is hosting Minecraft Server Controller.
topics.title: The port forward may point to the wrong target device

suggestedNextActions: Verify the server is running and reachable on the local network first.
Review macOS firewall or security-tool rules.
Re-test from outside your network after confirming local connectivity.
topics.summary: A correct router rule is not enough if the host still rejects inbound traffic.
topics.title: The Mac firewall or another filter may still be blocking traffic

suggestedNextActions: Confirm which game mode you are exposing.
Use TCP for Java and UDP for Bedrock unless your specific setup says otherwise.
Check whether both Java and Bedrock need separate rules.
topics.summary: Java usually needs TCP 25565. Bedrock usually needs UDP 19132.
topics.title: The protocol may be wrong

suggestedNextActions: Press Save / Apply in the forwarding page.
If the router asks to reboot, do it.
Re-test after the router is fully back online.
topics.summary: Some firmware does not activate the new rule immediately.
topics.title: The router may need a save/apply cycle or reboot

suggestedNextActions: Check whether you have the router admin login.
Ask the network owner or ISP whether forwarding is allowed.
Use a fallback remote-access solution if direct forwarding is blocked.
topics.summary: Some ISP, dorm, apartment, or managed-network environments lock down forwarding.
topics.title: You may not have permission to change router settings
